Harms of POCUS in Addition to the Standard Diagnostic Pathway or as a Replacement Diagnostic Test No studies reported direct complications due to POCUS or the downstream consequences of false-positive or false-negative results from POCUS or additional diagnos-tic interventions because of incidental ﬁndings. Few studies reported on indeterminate sonography results.
Values and Preferences No relevant literature was identiﬁed that assessed the values and preferences of patients with dyspnea for the selected outcomes.
Feedback from the CGC Public Panel showed prefer-ences trending in favor of adding POCUS to the standard diagnostic pathway, mostly because of the ﬁndings for correctness of diagnosis. For POCUS as a replacement test, most CGC Public Panel members responded that they would not be willing to undergo POCUS.
Costs No studies were identiﬁed that reported on the costs of POCUS compared with standard diagnostic pathways in the United States. Table 3 presents the Medicare national average reimbursement rates by condition.
MULTIPLE CHRONIC CONDITIONS: CLINICAL CONSIDERATIONS Many (n = 34) of the studies evaluated for this guideline included patients with 2 or more chronic conditions; thus, these recommendations likely apply to those with multiple chronic conditions. There may be differences in pretest probability depending on the individual clinical situation that would affect the test accuracy of POCUS in addition to or as a replacement for the standard diagnostic pathway.

AREAS OF NO EVIDENCE No studies provided information for the following out-comes when POCUS was used in addition to the standard diagnostic pathway or as a replacement test in patients with acute dyspnea: quality of life, admissions to intensive care units, and disease-speciﬁc health outcomes (unneces-sary use of antibiotics, need to use breathing support, time to referral, and lung computed tomography [proportion of patients]). No studies reported the consequences of false-positive or false-negative ﬁndings from POCUS in addition to the standard diagnostic pathway or as a replacement test, including additional or downstream testing.
RECOMMENDATION Supplement 2 (available at Annals.org) presents a graphic summary of the recommendation, evidence and rationale, and clinical considerations.
Recommendation: ACP suggests that clinicians may use point-of-care ultrasonography in addition to the standard diagnostic pathway when there is diagnostic uncertainty in patients with acute dyspnea in emergency department or inpatient settings (conditional recommen-dation; low-certainty evidence).
Rationale The rationale to add POCUS to the standard diagnos-tic pathway is largely based on diagnostic accuracy stud-ies and encompasses several considerations.
First, POCUS increased the proportion of correct diagnoses by 32% when used in addition to the standard diagnostic pathway (moderate-certainty evidence). Second, the test accuracy, particularly sensitivity, of standard diagnostic testing with the addition of POCUS is better than the test accuracy of standard diagnostic pathway alone without a substantial tradeoff in speciﬁcity (low-certainty evidence) (Table 1). The test accuracy of POCUS is generally accept-able, particularly for diagnosis of congestive heart failure or pleural effusion, although the usefulness of POCUS varies somewhat according to the underlying disease (Table 1 and Figure 2; see Clinical Considerations). Third, it is unlikely that POCUS is directly associated with serious harms. Finally, POCUS is not a high-cost test (Table 3). The CGC graded this as a conditional recommenda-tion because there was limited evidence examining the effect of POCUS on health outcomes, and there are many uncertainties related to variation in testing proto-cols, training, clinician experience, clinical setting, and equipment.
Limited evidence on health outcomes showed that POCUS did not reduce hospital length of stay or readmissions (moderate-certainty evidence).
However, there was no increase in length of stay with the addition of POCUS. The CGC determined that the lack of demonstrated effects on other health outcomes was ei-ther of low certainty or insufﬁcient and thus does not pre-clude clinically meaningful beneﬁts, especially given the supporting evidence on correctness of diagnosis and test accuracy as well as the lack of evidence of serious harms or high costs.
CLINICAL CONSIDERATIONS • The included studies enrolled adult patients present-ing in EDs and inpatient settings with dyspnea as a primary symptom (unspeciﬁed acute dyspnea) and who were later conﬁrmed to have 1 of the conditions of interest (congestive heart failure [including pulmo-nary edema], pleural effusion, pneumonia, pneumo-thorax, or pulmonary embolism).
• Findings may differ in outpatient settings. Thus, our recommendation applies to EDs and inpatient settings.
• The systematic review excluded studies that included patients with other medical conditions that can cause dyspnea (for example, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, acute coronary symptoms, and trauma) if the patients were not also conﬁrmed to have 1 of the conditions of interest.
• This recommendation does not apply to handheld devices; evidence from 1 high risk of bias study is very uncertain (insufﬁcient) about the effect of handheld POCUS devices in addition to the standard pathway on health, diagnostic, and treatment outcomes. Future research is needed to assess the effectiveness, harms, and diagnostic accuracy characteristics of handheld devices.
• Clinicians who use POCUS should be trained in the use and interpretation of ﬁndings and ongoing care quality assessment. This is an important area for future research: In the included studies, the experience and training of POCUS operators varied and reporting was limited.
• As with any diagnostic test, this recommendation applies to clinical scenarios where there is diagnostic uncertainty. Clinicians should understand and con-sider that the test accuracy of POCUS varies accord-ing to the likelihood of underlying diseases.
• Figure 2 shows that, using the prevalence estimates of various conditions reported in the studies, the rate of false-positive test results for pneumonia and pulmo-nary embolism may be higher than what many clini-cians and patients are comfortable with, especially because false-positive results for these conditions may lead to unnecessary use of anticoagulation and antibiotics.

APPENDIX: DETAILED METHODS OF THE SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND GUIDELINE Cochrane Austria at Danube University Krems con-ducted the supporting systematic review. Details of the ACP guideline development process can be found in ACP's methods articles (8, 9). Disclosure of interests and management of any conﬂicts can be found at https:// www.acponline.org/clinical_information/guidelines/ guidelines/conﬂicts_cgc.htm.
Key Questions Addressed Key question 1: In patients with acute dyspnea, what are the beneﬁcial and harmful health effects of POCUS plus clinical examination compared with clinical exami-nation alone?
Key question 2: What is the diagnostic test accuracy of POCUS in patients with acute dyspnea to detect con-gestive heart failure, pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax as the underlying cause of acute dyspnea?
Search Strategy of Systematic Review Reviewers searched several databases for studies and systematic reviews published in English from 2004 to August 2020.
Quality Assessment, Synthesis, and Overall Certainty of Evidence Reviewers used the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool (31) and the QUADAS-2 (Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2) tool (32) to assess the risk of bias for randomized controlled trials and diagnostic accuracy studies, respectively.
Population Studied Adult patients with unspeciﬁed acute dyspnea or acute dyspnea due to a suspected diagnosis of congestive heart failure (including pulmonary edema), pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax.
Interventions Evaluated Bedside POCUS (trolley- or cart-based, compact–hand-held, or application-based) in addition to clinical examina-tion with or without a standard diagnostic pathway.
Comparators Standard diagnostic pathway without POCUS; refer-ence tests: chest radiography, echocardiography, labora-tory values for congestive heart failure, chest radiography and computed tomography scan for pleural effusion and pneumonia, chest radiography for pneumothorax, and computed tomography pulmonary angiography and ven-tilation perfusion scanning for pulmonary embolism.
Outcomes Members of the CGC (clinicians and nonclinician public members) and the CGC Public Panel members were asked a priori to independently rate the impor-tance of evaluated outcomes.
Setting Hospital settings (ED, intensive care units, and nonin-tensive care settings) in countries with a “very high” Human Development Index.
Target Audience The target audience is all clinicians.
Target Patient Population The target patient population is adult patients with acute dyspnea in ED or inpatient settings.
Public or Patient Involvement The development of this guideline also included per-spectives, values, and preferences of 2 nonphysician CGC members who represent the public and a 7-member CGC Public Panel. In addition, the CGC Public Panel was also surveyed to assess their preferences with regards of the intervention options.
Annals of Internal Medicine Annals.org Cost Search ACP staff searched PubMed (MEDLINE) from incep-tion to February 2020. ACP staff searched several other databases (National Health Service Economic Evaluation Database, Database of Abstracts of Reviews of Effects, and the Health Technology Assessment database) from inception through 2015, at which point the databases stopped adding records. The search used a modiﬁed search string strategy from the clinical effectiveness review that added cost, resource use, and economic search terms as identiﬁed by the Canadian Agency for Drugs and Technologies in Health Information Services Filters Working Group.
ACP staff used the Medicare Fee Schedules to identify Medicare reimbursements fees for POCUS and other tests included in the standard diagnostic work-up for the included conditions. The search yielded 779 citations, of which 6 were selected for full-text review.
Peer Review The supporting systematic review and guideline each had a peer review process through the journal. The guideline was posted online for comments from ACP Regents and ACP Governors, who represent internal medicine and its subspecialty physician members at the national and international levels.

### Author Credentials

Editor: Sarkis Kouyoumjian, MD, FACEP Clerkship Director, Wayne State University, Detroit, MI

---

### Case Study

An ambulance arrives to your Emergency Department with a 60-year-old woman who reports she is having difficulty breathing.  Her vital signs en route were: BP 190/100, HR 118, RR 34, and SpO2 87% on RA.  As they move her off of the stretcher, you notice that she’s breathing fast, she isn’t talking, and her shoulders and abdomen move with each breath.

**Objectives**

1. Describe the initial approach to a patient in respiratory distress
2. Discuss initial management options for a patient in respiratory distress
3. List the immediate life-threatening causes of shortness of breath

### --- Introduction

Shortness of breath is a very common cause of Emergency Department visits.  In the United States, pneumonia, COPD exacerbation, heart failure exacerbation and dysrhythmias round out the top five reasons for hospital admission in patients 45 and older, after chest pain.  All of those conditions, and many others, can cause shortness of breath, which makes diagnosing the root cause difficult. It is a nonspecific symptom with many possible causes and degrees of severity, making the evaluation of these patients challenging.   In many cases, treatment/stabilization may actually precede establishing a final diagnosis.  It is important to consider the critical diagnoses in your evaluation and look for patterns in the history and physical exam.  Additional tests can be helpful in establishing a diagnosis or excluding alternative diagnoses.

### --- Initial Actions and Primary Survey

#### General Impression

Patients with a chief complaint of shortness of breath can vary in their degree of distress at initial presentation.  Like many other complaints in the ED, the assessment begins with, “What do I see when I walk into the room?”  Gaining that initial general impression within the first few seconds/minutes is critical—you may find you need to intervene to stabilize your patient before you have enough information to make a final diagnosis.

Our initial general impression of this patient is that she has abnormal vital signs, is breathing rapidly and is in severe distress.  We should prepare ourselves for immediate intervention.

#### First Steps

Having additional help from nurses, medics, or other ED staff is tremendously useful.  While you are assessing your patient’s ABCs, you should request the following to occur simultaneously:

* Full set of vital signs including BP, HR, RR, SpO2 and temperature
* Oxygen application via nasal cannula, non-rebreather mask, or bag-valve mask if patient requires assisted ventilations (not breathing adequately on their own)
* Cardiac and pulse oximetry monitoring
* IV access, including blood draw for ABG/VBG and other routine testing
* In some cases, obtaining an EKG may be useful as well

If your patient fails to respond to oxygen administration and is not breathing adequately, you may need to consider more aggressive treatment with non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) or intubation.

The patient’s first set of vital signs in the ED is consistent with those reported by EMS.  She is placed on a non-rebreather mask at 15 LPM without significant improvement in her level of distress or her oxygen saturation.  IV access is obtained, and patient is placed on the monitor.  EKG shows sinus tachycardia.  Her mental status is normal, however, and she is able to protect her airway.  Respiratory therapy is paged to respond with a BiPAP machine.

|  |
| --- |
| Indications for Non-invasive Ventilation |
| Consider NIPPV in patients with | When NOT to use NIPPV |
| Moderate to severe dyspnea Accessory muscle use Paradoxical abdominal movement Fatigue RR > 25 bpm pH < 7.35, pCO2 >45 | Respiratory arrest/absent respiratory drive Hemodynamic instability Aspiration Risk Airway obstruction Unable to tolerate mask Mask does not fit Altered mental status |

### --- History and Physical Exam

In developing a working diagnosis, the history can often provide clues to the etiology of your patient’s symptoms.  If the patient is unable to answer questions because of their respiratory distress, ask the paramedics or family members if they have any useful information.  They may have insight into the patient’s past medical history or pertinent events leading up to the patient’s encounter.  Medications can be extremely helpful. For example, a person with an albuterol inhaler is likely to have COPD/asthma history or a person with a furosemide prescription may have a history of heart failure.

Some key elements of the history:

* Did the shortness of breath begin suddenly?  If so, consider pulmonary embolism or spontaneous pneumothorax.  A gradual onset of symptoms is more suggestive for COPD, pneumonia, or congestive heart failure.
* Is the shortness of breath chronic or recurrent?  Many chronic disease processes can acutely worsen from time to time.  Your patient may even be able to tell you that his or her symptoms are similar to the last episode of asthma/COPD/CHF/pneumonia/etc.
* Is the shortness of breath positional or exertional?  Orthopnea is typically thought of as a symptom of CHF but can also occur in COPD, neuromuscular disorders, pleural/pericardial effusions, or ascites.  Exertional dyspnea can also have multiple causes including primary pulmonary disease, cardiac ischemia, or anemia.
* Were there any precipitating events?  Shortness of breath occurring after an environmental or known allergen exposure can be a clue in diagnosing an allergic reaction.  Similarly, recent hospitalization or prolonged travel may raise your suspicion for a PE.
* Does your patient have any pertinent past medical history?  As stated above, a history of asthma, COPD, or CHF, for example, can suggest a cause for your patient’s symptoms.  Suspicion for developing angioedema may be higher if your patient has a history of hypertension treated with an ACE inhibitor.

The physical exam can also be incredibly helpful in determining a cause for your patient’s symptoms.  Learning to recognize patterns that support your history can make your evaluation more efficient.

* Visible swelling in the upper airway can point to an allergic reaction or angioedema.  Voice changes, stridor, and drooling are ominous signs concerning for impending airway obstruction and can be related to an infection, allergic reaction, or foreign body.
* Focally absent or diminished breath sounds on auscultation can suggest an infectious consolidation, effusion, or pneumothorax.
* Wheezing can be attributed to bronchospastic processes, such as asthma, COPD, and anaphylaxis.
* Rales can be found in pneumonia, PE, and pleural effusions.  Rales in the setting of JVD and peripheral edema can be suspicious for CHF.
* Unilateral leg swelling and tenderness raises suspicion for a DVT/PE.
* Signs of chest trauma, including crepitus, bruising, and tenderness can be suggestive of pneumothorax, hemothorax, or pulmonary contusion.
* “Tripoding,” or use of accessory muscles may be less helpful in determining the etiology, but can signal impending respiratory failure and need for immediate intervention.

EMS reports that our patient has been out of her medications for several weeks, which include multiple antihypertensives and a diuretic.  On physical examination, she has bilateral rales to the level of her shoulder blades, pitting edema in both legs, and JVD.  She is placed on BiPAP, given nitroglycerin, and her symptoms and vital signs begin to improve.

### --- Diagnostic Testing

After the initial assessment and stabilization of your patient, additional tests can be used to confirm a diagnosis or exclude other potential life-threatening diagnoses.

* An EKG can be used to assess for cardiac ischemia, dysrhythmia, PE, pericarditis, and pericardial effusion.
* Chest x-rays are often obtained as portable (bedside) AP views in unstable patients and as PA/lateral views in stable patients who can be transported to radiology.  They can reveal a wide array of pathologies, including pneumonia, pleural effusions, pneumothorax, and chest wall injuries.
* Chest CTs can be performed to evaluate for atypical infections, traumatic injuries, pulmonary emboli, and aortic pathologies.
* Beside ultrasonography is often the fastest way to gather additional information.  Ultrasound examination of the lungs can identify a pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, pleural effusion, or consolidation.  Cardiac views can identify left ventricular dysfunction such as in CHF, right heart strain such as in PE or pulmonary hypertension, pericardial effusions, and tamponade.  Ultrasound is also used to evaluate for lower extremity DVTs.
* Laboratory tests can provide additional information to support a diagnosis or assist in the workup (e.g. d-dimer to exclude low probability PE, BNP to assess for CHF exacerbation, serial cardiac enzymes to exclude MI).
* ABG analysis may be necessary to determine a patient’s true oxygenation status.  Typically, a standard SpO2 measurement with a reliable waveform is adequate to determine the patient’s oxygenation status.  However, a reliable waveform may be difficult to get in unstable patients who are combative, cold, diaphoretic, or who have otherwise unreliable SpO2 measurements.  In this situation, an ABG may be necessary to determine an accurate partial pressure of oxygen and oxygen saturation. The ABG will also give accurate partial pressure of carbon dioxide.  However, ABGs require an arterial puncture to obtain and therefore may not be as readily available as a VBG.
* VBGs can be obtained with standard venipuncture during IV insertion.  The VBG is critical to determine a patient’s partial pressure of carbon dioxide.  Elevated levels of venous CO2 in a tachypneic patient typically indicates a bronchospastic process such as asthma or COPD.  However, in patients with decreased respiratory drive this may represent poor overall ventilation.

A bedside ultrasound is done immediately following the physical exam.  Cardiac views show a severely depressed ejection fraction and lung windows show diffuse B-lines consistent with pulmonary edema.  She is placed on BiPAP, given nitroglycerin, and her symptoms and vital signs begin to improve.

### --- Differential Diagnosis

Critical diagnoses (and general management options) to consider in patients with respiratory distress include:

* [Acute congestive heart failure exacerbation](http://saem.org/cdem/education/online-education/m4-curriculum/group-m4-cardiovascular/congestive-heart-failure) – supplemental O2, PPV, nitrates, diuretics
* [Acute coronary syndrome](http://saem.org/cdem/education/online-education/m4-curriculum/group-m4-cardiovascular/acute-coronary-syndromes) – aspirin, antiplatelet agents, anticoagulation, reperfusion therapy
* Anaphylaxis – epinephrine, beta-agonists, antihistamines, steroids
* [Asthma](http://saem.org/cdem/education/online-education/m4-curriculum/group-m4-respiratory/asthma)/[COPD](http://saem.org/cdem/education/online-education/m4-curriculum/group-m4-respiratory/copd) exacerbation – PPV, beta-agonists, steroids
* Cardiac tamponade – pericardiocentesis
* Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema – supplemental O2, PPV, diuretics, antibiotics
* [Pulmonary embolism](http://saem.org/cdem/education/online-education/m4-curriculum/group-m4-cardiovascular/pulmonary-embolus) – anticoagulation, lytic agents (systemic or catheter directed), thrombectomy
* [Pneumonia](http://saem.org/cdem/education/online-education/m4-curriculum/group-m4-respiratory/pneumonia) – antibiotics, supplemental O2, PPV
* [Pneumothorax](http://saem.org/cdem/education/online-education/m4-curriculum/group-m4-respiratory/pneumothorax)/tension pneumothorax – needle decompression, tube thoracostomy
* Upper airway obstruction – early intubation for airway protection (alternative: cricothyrotomy), treat underlying cause

### --- Pearls & Pitfalls

* Your assessment of the patient’s work of breathing will largely determine your initial approach to management.  Severely ill patients will require immediate escalation of treatment, while in less sick patients it may be reasonable to wait on diagnostics before beginning therapeutic interventions.
* Bedside ultrasonography has become a powerful tool in the diagnosis of acute dyspnea.  Using ultrasound early in the care of the dyspneic patient can help risk stratify patients for multiple emergent causes including: acute heart failure exacerbation, pulmonary edema, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, pericardial effusion, and pulmonary embolus.
* While information provided by EMS and family can play an important role in history gathering, avoid temptation to anchor your diagnosis on information that may ultimately be flawed or otherwise irrelevant.

### --- Case Study Resolution

With continued NIPPV and nitrate therapy, our patient’s degree of respiratory distress improves significantly, and she is able to avoid intubation.  She is admitted to the hospital for an acute CHF exacerbation and is restarted on her home medications.  After several days of additional diuresis, she feels back to normal and is discharged home.

Circulation 2026; 153:e977. [...] Although frequently used, the value of high-flow oxygen delivered via nasal cannulae (HFNC) in patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure remains unclear. In a randomized trial of 1110 such patients, HFNC did not reduce 28-day mortality compared with low-flow oxygen . HFNC led to a non-significant reduction in the intubation rate at 28 days (42.4 versus 48.4 percent), and rapidly improved patients' respiratory rates, dyspnea, and carbon dioxide levels. These data support our practice of administering HFNC only to patients with advanced oxygen needs (eg, >6 L/minute) rather than routine administration. ADULT RESUSCITATION

Anticoagulation in extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (July 2026)

Data guiding anticoagulation during extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) are limited. In a recent randomized trial of 330 patients (60 percent venoarterial ECMO, 40 percent venovenous ECMO), low-dose [unfractionated heparin](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/heparin-unfractionated-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) (UFH) resulted in a nonsignificant reduction in severe bleeding compared with standard-dose UFH (58 versus 65 percent), without increasing severe thromboembolic complications (11 versus 10 percent) [[1](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/1)]. Although promising, interpretation is limited because the standard-dose regimen may not reflect current practice, anti-factor Xa monitoring was inconsistent and the study was open label. More robust data are needed before we can routinely use low-dose UFH for anticoagulating ECMO patients. (See ["Extracorporeal life support in adults: Management of venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA ECMO)", section on 'Anticoagulation'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/extracorporeal-life-support-in-adults-management-of-venoarterial-extracorporeal-membrane-oxygenation-va-ecmo?sectionName=Anticoagulation&topicRef=8365&anchor=H372499665&source=see_link#H372499665).)

Liberal versus restrictive oxygenation targets after cardiac arrest (June 2026)

The optimal peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO 2) target in mechanically ventilated cardiac arrest survivors is uncertain. In a recent randomized trial of 1840 such patients targeting an SpO₂ of 95 percent with an allowable minimum fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO₂) of 0.21 resulted in similar rates of favorable functional outcomes, mortality, and length of stay at 180 days compared with higher oxygen targets and allowable minimum FiO₂ of 0.3, without and increase in adverse events [[2](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/2)]. These data support our practice of targeting an SpO2 at the lower end of the 95 to 98 percent range. (See ["Intensive care unit management of the intubated post-cardiac arrest adult patient", section on 'Airway, ventilation, and oxygen targets'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/intensive-care-unit-management-of-the-intubated-post-cardiac-arrest-adult-patient?sectionName=Airway%2C+ventilation%2C+and+oxygen+targets&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3262398353&source=see_link#H3262398353).)

Catheter-directed thrombolysis versus anticoagulation in pulmonary embolism (March 2026)

In patients with intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism (PE; ie, biochemical and imaging evidence of right ventricle [RV] dysfunction), limited data suggest that catheter-directed thrombolysis improves RV function compared with anticoagulation alone, but does not improve mortality. In a recent randomized trial of 544 patients with intermediate-high-risk PE, ultrasound-facilitated, catheter-directed thrombolysis with [alteplase](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/alteplase-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) reduced the composite outcome of PE-related death, cardiorespiratory decompensation, or symptomatic PE recurrence compared with anticoagulation alone (4 versus 10 percent); this difference was driven primarily by fewer episodes of decompensation (3.7 versus 10.3 percent) [[3](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/3)]. Major bleeding was numerically higher in the alteplase group (4 versus 2 percent) but was not statistically significant, and the difference in RV size at 48 hours between the two groups was also not significant. Interpretation is limited by low event rates, lack of blinding, and underrepresentation of patients >75 years. However, these data support our practice of performing catheter-directed therapies in patients with intermediate-high-risk PE. (See ["Acute pulmonary embolism in adults: Reperfusion therapy in intermediate- and high-risk patients", section on 'Catheter-directed thrombolysis'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-pulmonary-embolism-in-adults-reperfusion-therapy-in-intermediate-and-high-risk-patients?sectionName=Catheter-directed+thrombolysis&topicRef=8365&anchor=H4140125415&source=see_link#H4140125415).)

Updated international Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines (March 2026)

The Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines have recently been updated [[4](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/4)]. The guidelines suggested that, while a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg should be targeted, a range of 60 to 70 mmHg is practical for most adults with sepsis. The guidelines also emphasized the importance of screening tools for early detection and management of sepsis, while discouraging both overly aggressive fluid resuscitation and empiric treatment for fungal and anaerobic bacterial infections, especially when suspicion is low. The guidelines encouraged active fluid removal (in the later phases of shock), rapid de-escalation of antimicrobials and, in mechanically ventilated patients, the use of selective digestive tract decontamination to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia. We agree with these recommendations. (See ["Evaluation and management of suspected sepsis and septic shock in adults", section on 'Introduction'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-suspected-sepsis-and-septic-shock-in-adults?sectionName=INTRODUCTION&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1&source=see_link#H1).)

Joint European and United States definition of refractory septic shock (March 2026)

Although sepsis and septic shock have widely accepted definitions, there has not been consensus regarding the definition of "refractory" septic shock. The Society of Critical Care Medicine and European Society of Intensive Care Medicine have recently proposed criteria defining refractory septic shock by the presence of (1) persistently elevated lactate concentration (>2 mmol/L [>18 mg/dL]) and/or prolonged capillary refill time, (2) lack of response to fluid resuscitation, (3) a norepinephrine base equivalent dose >0.5 micrograms per kilogram per minute, and (4) in those with suspected mixed shock, critical care ultrasound should be used to confirm lack of response to fluids and to exclude other etiologies for shock [[5](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/5)]. The impact of this definition on patient outcomes, such as survival, remains undetermined. (See ["Sepsis syndromes in adults: Epidemiology, definitions, clinical presentation, diagnosis, and prognosis", section on 'Septic shock'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/sepsis-syndromes-in-adults-epidemiology-definitions-clinical-presentation-diagnosis-and-prognosis?sectionName=Septic+shock&topicRef=8365&anchor=H8&source=see_link#H8).)

High-flow oxygen does not affect mortality in hypoxemic respiratory failure (March 2026)

Although frequently used, the value of high-flow oxygen delivered via nasal cannulae (HFNC) in patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure remains unclear. In a randomized trial of 1110 such patients, HFNC did not reduce 28-day mortality compared with low-flow oxygen [[6](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/6)]. HFNC led to a non-significant reduction in the intubation rate at 28 days (42.4 versus 48.4 percent), and rapidly improved patients' respiratory rates, dyspnea, and carbon dioxide levels. These data support our practice of administering HFNC only to patients with advanced oxygen needs (eg, >6 L/minute) rather than routine administration. (See ["Evaluation and management of the nonventilated, hospitalized adult patient with acute hypoxemia", section on 'Humidified, high-flow oxygen delivered via nasal cannulae (HFNC)'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-the-nonventilated-hospitalized-adult-patient-with-acute-hypoxemia?sectionName=Humidified%2C+high-flow+oxygen+delivered+via+nasal+cannulae+%28HFNC%29&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3611214250&source=see_link#H3611214250).)

ENVIRONMENTAL EMERGENCIES

Iloprost for amputation prevention in frostbite (May 2026)

[Iloprost](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/iloprost-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) is a prostacyclin analog that is indicated for the treatment of grade 3 or 4 frostbite (ie, cyanosis that extends proximal to the distal phalanx after rewarming), but supporting evidence is limited. In a study with over 250 patients (80 receiving iloprost) in two Canadian regions that differed in routine iloprost use but with a standardized frostbite care pathway, iloprost was associated with a lower amputation rate for grade 3 frostbite (30 versus 53 percent) but not for grade 2 and 4 frostbite; patients receiving a higher total iloprost dose were less likely to have amputations [[7](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/7)]. In 40 patients with grade 4 frostbite, iloprost treatment was associated with fewer finger and toe segment amputations (40 versus 51 percent and 47 versus 58 percent, respectively). These findings support our recommendation for iloprost in patients with severe frostbite. (See ["Frostbite: Acute care and prevention", section on 'Iloprost within 72 hours'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/frostbite-acute-care-and-prevention?sectionName=Iloprost+within+72+hours&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1902794625&source=see_link#H1902794625).)

Microorganisms in children with freshwater drowning-associated pneumonia (February 2026)

Infection with gram-negative organisms, especially _Aeromonas_ species, is predominantly reported in patients with drowning-associated pneumonia (DAP). In a study from China of over 70 children with freshwater DAP in a pediatric intensive care unit, _Staphylococcus aureus_ was the most isolated organism [[8](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/8)]. Other common pathogens included _Mycoplasma pneumoniae_, _Streptococcus pneumoniae_, _Haemophilus influenzae_, _Klebsiella pneumoniae_, _Candida albicans_, and rhinovirus. These findings highlight the need for an empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic regimen, including coverage of gram-positive bacteria, in children with suspected DAP. (See ["Drowning (submersion injuries)", section on 'Pneumonia'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/drowning-submersion-injuries?sectionName=Pneumonia&topicRef=8365&anchor=H809358478&source=see_link#H809358478).)

Effectiveness of defibrillation in patients with hypothermia and nonperfusing shockable rhythm (February 2026)

Patients with hypothermia and nonperfusing shockable arrhythmias are less likely to have return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) with defibrillation at a core temperature <30°C (86°F). Current recommendations are to attempt defibrillation with up to three shocks but withhold further attempts pending rewarming since cold myocardium can potentially be injured. A registry-based study with almost 40 patients with cardiac arrest, a shockable rhythm, and core temperature <30°C found that ROSC was more likely if defibrillation was performed during rewarming, as compared with before rewarming (100 versus 25 percent) [[9](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/9)]. Defibrillation during extracorporeal life support (ECLS) had a fivefold increase in odds of ROSC. These findings support our recommendations to attempt defibrillation even with temperature <30°C and to not withhold defibrillation during ECLS rewarming at temperature >25°C (77°F). (See ["Accidental hypothermia in adults: Management", section on 'Ventricular arrhythmias or asystole'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/accidental-hypothermia-in-adults-management?sectionName=Ventricular+arrhythmias+or+asystole&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1808505299&source=see_link#H1808505299).)

Acute hypersensitivity reactions from rattlesnake antivenom in alpha-gal endemic region (February 2026)

CroFab and Anavip, antivenoms used to treat Crotalinae snakebite envenomation, can potentially cause severe allergic reactions. Anavip contains more of the carbohydrate moiety galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose (which is responsible for alpha-gal syndrome) compared with CroFab. A study with over 200 patients in Arkansas (a state with a high rate of alpha-gal sensitization) who received either Anavip or CroFab found that Anavip was associated with increased adverse drug reactions (including presumed anaphylaxis) compared with CroFab (22 versus 4 percent) [[10](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/10)]. Basophil activation testing from individuals with known alpha-gal syndrome found that Anavip more potently activated alpha-gal sensitized basophils. Clinicians who treat snakebite victims in regions with high rates of alpha-gal sensitization must be ready to manage anaphylaxis following antivenom (especially Anavip) administration. (See ["Bites by Crotalinae snakes (rattlesnakes, cottonmouths [water moccasins], or copperheads) in the United States: Management", section on 'Acute antivenom hypersensitivity reactions'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/bites-by-crotalinae-snakes-rattlesnakes-cottonmouths-water-moccasins-or-copperheads-in-the-united-states-management?sectionName=Acute+antivenom+hypersensitivity+reactions&topicRef=8365&anchor=H4098260420&source=see_link#H4098260420).)

GENERAL ADULT EMERGENCY MEDICINE

YEARS criteria for pulmonary embolism exclusion in patients with active cancer (July 2026)

The YEARS criteria adjusts D-dimer cutoffs for excluding pulmonary embolism (PE) based on pretest probability, but it is unknown whether it can be utilized in patients with active cancer. In a randomized trial including 698 patients with active cancer suspected of having a PE, the diagnostic failure rate at 90 days was similar in patients evaluated by the YEARS algorithm compared with a standard chest computed tomography pulmonary angiogram (1.8 versus 5 percent) [[11](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/11)]. Limitations of the study included an open-label design, exclusion of patients with a life expectancy <3 months, lack of subgroup analysis by cancer site and stage, and early cessation of the study. Nonetheless, these results suggest that YEARS may be used to exclude PE in patients with active cancer, although further study and validation is needed. (See ["Clinical presentation and diagnostic evaluation of the nonpregnant adult with suspected acute pulmonary embolism", section on 'Alternative (adjusted) D-dimer cutoffs with or without YEARS'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/clinical-presentation-and-diagnostic-evaluation-of-the-nonpregnant-adult-with-suspected-acute-pulmonary-embolism?sectionName=Alternative+%28adjusted%29+D-dimer+cutoffs+with+or+without+YEARS&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2075009429&source=see_link#H2075009429).)

Cyclosporiasis outbreak in the United States (July 2026)

Cyclosporiasis is a parasitic infection characterized by watery diarrhea, usually caused by ingestion of contaminated food. In May 2026, a large outbreak of cyclosporiasis was recognized in the United States [[12](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/12)]. The source of the cases appears to be related to the ingestion of a widely distributed contaminated lettuce product [[13](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/13)]. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention advises clinicians to consider cyclosporiasis in the diagnosis of patients presenting with watery diarrhea, ask the laboratory to specifically test stool for Cyclospora spp. (with PCR, if available), and ask patients with suspected or confirmed cyclosporiasis about their recent food and travel history. Up-to-date information on the cyclosporiasis outbreak in the United States can be found on the [CDC cyclosporiasis page.](https://www.uptodate.com/external-redirect?target_url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cdc.gov%2Fcyclosporiasis%2Fphp%2Fsurveillance%2Findex.html&token=t7NCXpgOToFkdCMjAwY9q6i4%2BvYZVJy0risdHMpqEf106dXhWudmk2P8tRKy0awIS4MtcwKnOZ3Rcfrqurs4668AtSQsFLDSFqHlsS1NKKs%3D&TOPIC_ID=8365) (See ["_Cyclospora_ infection", section on 'Epidemiology'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/cyclospora-infection?sectionName=EPIDEMIOLOGY&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2&source=see_link#H2).)

Marine toxin disease outbreaks in the United States (July 2026)

Marine toxins are an important cause of noninfectious foodborne disease outbreaks. Scombroid poisoning causes flushing, a warmth sensation, and an erythematous, urticarial rash often prominent on the face and upper torso soon after ingestion of improperly stored fish. Ciguatera poisoning causes a gastrointestinal illness followed by delayed onset neurologic symptoms such as paresthesias and temperature-related dysesthesias. A study of the United States Foodborne Disease Outbreak Surveillance System found that 402 marine toxin outbreaks were reported between 2011 and 2023, representing 1280 affected individuals; nearly all outbreaks implicated scombroid or ciguatoxin [[14](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/14)]. These findings underscore the need to inquire about recent fish consumption in patients presenting with characteristic clinical features and may help inform public health surveillance and prevention efforts. (See ["Scombroid (histamine) poisoning", section on 'Epidemiology'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/scombroid-histamine-poisoning?sectionName=EPIDEMIOLOGY&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1057420&source=see_link#H1057420) and ["Ciguatera fish poisoning", section on 'Epidemiology'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/ciguatera-fish-poisoning?sectionName=EPIDEMIOLOGY&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3603702&source=see_link#H3603702).)

American Thoracic Society guidelines on noninvasive respiratory support (July 2026)

The American Thoracic Society (ATS) recently issued guidelines on the use of noninvasive respiratory support for patients with acute respiratory failure, in whom low-flow oxygen is insufficient [[15](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/15)]. The ATS recommends using high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) oxygen for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure and suggests noninvasive ventilation (NIV) for acute hypercapnic respiratory failure. The ATS also suggests either modality for preoxygenation prior to endotracheal intubation; post-extubation, the ATS suggests HFNC for low-risk patients and NIV for high-risk patients. We agree with these recommendations. (See ["Evaluation and management of the nonventilated, hospitalized adult patient with acute hypoxemia", section on 'Oxygen and respiratory support'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-the-nonventilated-hospitalized-adult-patient-with-acute-hypoxemia?sectionName=Oxygen+and+respiratory+support&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1642231459&source=see_link#H1642231459) and ["Noninvasive ventilation in adults with acute respiratory failure: Benefits and contraindications"](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/noninvasive-ventilation-in-adults-with-acute-respiratory-failure-benefits-and-contraindications?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) and ["Extubation management in the adult intensive care unit"](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/extubation-management-in-the-adult-intensive-care-unit?topicRef=8365&source=see_link).)

Fosphenytoin for trigeminal neuralgia attacks (May 2026)

Several pharmacologic options are available to treat acute trigeminal neuralgia (TN) pain, but available supporting evidence is limited. In a randomized trial that included 22 patients with acute TN symptoms, pain reduction on the numerical rating scale (0 for no pain up to 10 for worst pain) was greater at two hours among those assigned to [fosphenytoin](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/fosphenytoin-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) than placebo (-6.1 versus -2.4) [[16](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/16)]. Treatment consisted of a loading dose followed by once daily maintenance treatment for up to four days. Patients assigned to fosphenytoin also had a higher rate of >50 percent pain reduction and reduction in the frequency of attack recurrence, and treatment was generally well tolerated. These data provide clinical trial evidence to support the role of fosphenytoin for acute TN exacerbations. (See ["Trigeminal neuralgia", section on 'Acute rescue therapy for patients with breakthrough pain'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/trigeminal-neuralgia?sectionName=Acute+rescue+therapy+for+patients+with+breakthrough+pain&topicRef=8365&anchor=H372586115&source=see_link#H372586115).)

AHA/ACC guidelines for pulmonary embolism (March 2026)

Several societies, including the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC), have issued joint guidelines for the evaluation and management of pulmonary embolism (PE) [[17](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/17)]. The guidelines stratify patients by risk of PE-related death to facilitate management. Patients in category A (incidental PE), B (symptomatic PE with a low clinical severity score), and C (symptomatic PE with an elevated clinical severity score) require anticoagulation. Patients in category D (incipient cardiopulmonary failure) and E (cardiopulmonary failure) are candidates for reperfusion therapies (eg, thrombectomy or thrombolysis, if they have a low bleeding risk). We await adoption of this classification and encourage its use to facilitate management. (See ["Acute pulmonary embolism in adults: Treatment overview and prognosis", section on 'American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology/others'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-pulmonary-embolism-in-adults-treatment-overview-and-prognosis?sectionName=American+Heart+Association%2FAmerican+College+of+Cardiology%2Fothers&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2148862999&source=see_link#H2148862999).)

Pediatric sepsis hospitalization and mortality in the United States (March 2026)

New estimates of United States sepsis hospitalizations and in-hospital mortality based on a pediatric sepsis event definition derived from the 2024 Phoenix sepsis criteria have been reported using electronic-health record surveillance of clinical data from over 3.9 million pediatric hospitalizations (neonates excluded) from 2016 to 2023. The average annual hospital incidence of sepsis was 1.3 percent (over 18,000 annual cases); overall in-hospital mortality was 10.1 percent (over 1800 annual deaths) [[18,19](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/18,19)]. Annualized national estimates remained stable over the study period. These findings update prior sepsis estimates based upon older definitions of pediatric sepsis and confirm the high burden of pediatric illness due to sepsis in the United States. (See ["Sepsis in children: Definitions, clinical manifestations, and diagnosis", section on 'Burden of disease'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/sepsis-in-children-definitions-clinical-manifestations-and-diagnosis?sectionName=Burden+of+disease&topicRef=8365&anchor=H632992306&source=see_link#H632992306).)

PEDIATRIC RESUSCITATION

International guidelines for the management of pediatric sepsis and septic shock (May 2026)

The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Pediatric Guidelines for the management of sepsis and septic shock in children are available [[20](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/20)]. The guidelines reaffirm the prime importance of the rapid recognition of septic shock and treatment that includes timely administration of fluid bolus therapy, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics, and, in patients not responding to fluid bolus therapy, initiation of vasoactive medications (epinephrine or norepinephrine) ([algorithm 1](https://www.uptodate.com/content-not-available)). The 2026 guidelines also provide new recommendations that promote the use of blood lactate trends, lung and cardiac point-of-care ultrasound, and central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO 2 ≥ 70 percent) to monitor resuscitation. Our approach is consistent with these guidelines. (See ["Children with sepsis in resource-abundant settings: Rapid recognition and initial resuscitation (first hour)", section on 'Approach'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/children-with-sepsis-in-resource-abundant-settings-rapid-recognition-and-initial-resuscitation-first-hour?sectionName=Approach&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2493912177&source=see_link#H2493912177).)

Balanced crystalloid solution versus normal saline for children with septic shock (April 2026)

For children with septic shock, whether to administer balanced crystalloid solutions (BCS; for example, [lactated Ringer](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/lactated-ringer-solution-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link)'s) versus normal [saline](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/sodium-chloride-preparations-saline-and-oral-salt-tablets-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) (NS) during initial fluid resuscitation is unclear. In a new randomized trial of over 8400 children with suspected septic shock, the combined outcomes of death, initiation of renal-replacement therapy, and persistent kidney dysfunction at 30 days were not significantly different in patients who were assigned to fluid resuscitation for up to 48 hours with BCS (3.4 percent) versus NS (3 percent) [[21](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/21)]. Hyperchloremia and hypernatremia were more common in patients receiving NS; increased blood lactate was more common in patients receiving BCS. Otherwise, adverse effects were similar in both groups. These findings suggest that either BCS or NS is an appropriate choice for fluid resuscitation of children with septic shock. However, the results may not be generalizable to patients with hospital-acquired sepsis or those treated in resource-limited settings. (See ["Children with sepsis in resource-abundant settings: Rapid recognition and initial resuscitation (first hour)", section on 'Fluid resuscitation'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/children-with-sepsis-in-resource-abundant-settings-rapid-recognition-and-initial-resuscitation-first-hour?sectionName=Fluid+resuscitation&topicRef=8365&anchor=H19450206&source=see_link#H19450206).)

PRIMARY CARE ORTHOPEDICS AND SPORTS MEDICINE

Management of severely displaced distal radius fractures in children (April 2026)

For children with severely displaced distal radius fractures, the usual approach is fracture reduction and casting by a clinician or orthopedic surgeon with pediatric expertise. In a pragmatic trial of 750 children (4 to 10 years old) with severely displaced distal radial fractures, patients with markedly displaced Salter-Harris I or II physeal or metaphyseal fractures, were randomized to surgical reduction and casting versus casting alone [[22](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/22)]. At three months, functional outcomes, pain, and quality of life measured by validated scores as well as subjective cosmesis were significantly better in the surgical group. However, the difference in scores was small and less than minimally important differences for each outcome and became nonsignificant along with cosmesis at 12 months. These findings suggest that casting alone by an experienced clinician or orthopedic surgeon may be a reasonable option in children <10 years old with these injuries. However, we continue to support prompt reduction and casting pending further confirmation of these results. (See ["Distal forearm fractures in children: Initial management", section on 'Complete fracture'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/distal-forearm-fractures-in-children-initial-management?sectionName=Complete+fracture&topicRef=8365&anchor=H34&source=see_link#H34) and ["Distal forearm fractures in children: Initial management", section on 'Displaced Salter-Harris I or II fractures'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/distal-forearm-fractures-in-children-initial-management?sectionName=Displaced+Salter-Harris+I+or+II+fractures&topicRef=8365&anchor=H26&source=see_link#H26).)

Persistent symptoms of concussion in young children (March 2026)

In a prospective study, 235 young children (median age 2.4 years, 98 percent with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 15) were diagnosed with concussion in the emergency department (ED) based on the GCS score and ≥1 of the following: palpable skull fracture, headache (in verbal patients), altered mental status, or loss of consciousness [[23](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/23)]. At one month, 28 percent had persistent symptoms on a parent-reported symptoms score. This rate was significantly higher than in controls with orthopedic injuries undergoing ED evaluation and community children. On adjusted analysis, ED symptom severity was the primary predictor of persistent symptoms. These findings suggest that, similar to older children and adolescents, young children appear to have a significant risk of persistent symptoms of concussion after a mild head injury that appears to be associated with the severity of symptoms at initial evaluation. (See ["Concussion in children and adolescents: Management", section on 'Prognosis'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/concussion-in-children-and-adolescents-management?sectionName=PROGNOSIS&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2832537&source=see_link#H2832537).)

PROCEDURES

POCUS in infants and young children undergoing transurethral bladder catheterization (July 2026)

Transurethral bladder catheterization (TUBC) is the preferred method for obtaining urine specimens for culture in infants and young children who are not toilet trained; visualization of urine in the bladder with point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) prior to TUBC may facilitate collection. In a meta-analysis of three trials (337 children undergoing TUBC), first attempt success rate was higher for patients undergoing POCUS (89.7 versus 72.5 percent) and the rate of catheterization attempts resulting in no urine present ("dry taps") was lower (3.6 versus 23.9 percent) compared with patients undergoing TUBC without POCUS [[24](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/24)]. These findings confirm improved success rates reported in prior studies and support routine use of POCUS prior to TUBC in this population whenever available. (See ["Urine collection techniques in infants and children with suspected urinary tract infection", section on 'Transurethral bladder catheterization'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/urine-collection-techniques-in-infants-and-children-with-suspected-urinary-tract-infection?sectionName=Transurethral+bladder+catheterization&topicRef=8365&anchor=H678706983&source=see_link#H678706983).)

TOXICOLOGY

Severe hydrogen sulfide poisoning (June 2026)

Hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S) is a colorless gas with a rotten egg odor that potently inhibits mitochondrial respiration. It is a byproduct of microbial decomposition of organic matter (ie, "sewer gas") and various industrial processes. In a study of 168 patients with H 2 S poisoning reported to the Taiwan Poison Control Center, those working underground and in confined spaces were more likely to develop severe toxicity [[25](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/25)]. Early administration of [sodium nitrite](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/sodium-nitrite-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) was associated with potentially lower odds of death, but did not reach statistical significance. These findings should prompt clinicians to consider H 2 S poisoning in a patient with sudden loss of consciousness, lactic acidosis, and cardiovascular collapse who was working underground or in a confined space, and support our suggestion for treating these patients with sodium nitrite. (See ["Common occupational chemical exposures: General approach and management of selected exposures", section on 'Hydrogen sulfide'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/common-occupational-chemical-exposures-general-approach-and-management-of-selected-exposures?sectionName=Hydrogen+sulfide&topicRef=8365&anchor=H394318957&source=see_link#H394318957).)

Poisoning-related fatality from illicit substances in children and adolescents (May 2026)

Illicit substances such as opioids can result in poisoning-related fatality in pediatric patients. In an analysis conducted on national surveillance databases from the Centers for Disease Control, the rate of death from poisoning (including illicit drug overdoses) in children and adolescents aged 1 to 19 years increased by 12.7 percent from 2020 to 2023 [[26](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/26)]. In 2023, 1913 deaths were from illicit drug overdoses, and the majority (79.5 percent) were from [fentanyl](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/fentanyl-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link). These findings confirm that illicit substances remain a common cause of fatality in children and adolescents, and that ongoing educational and other preventive measures are warranted in this population. (See ["Poisoning in children: Prevention", section on 'Fatalities'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/poisoning-in-children-prevention?sectionName=Fatalities&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2&source=see_link#H2).)

Poisoning-related injury from ingested household products in young children (May 2026)

Ingested household products remain a common cause of poisoning-related injury in young children. An analysis of national surveillance data estimated that over 240,000 children aged ≤5 years were treated in United States emergency departments for injuries from exposure to household cleaning products from 2007 to 2022 [[27](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/27)]. Approximately 60 percent of injuries were from ingestion. The products and containers associated with the most injuries were bleach (30.1 percent), detergents (28.6 percent), detergent packets (33 percent), and spray bottles (28.2 percent). These findings highlight the importance of ongoing educational, regulatory, and product engineering measures to prevent injuries from ingested substances in pediatric patients. (See ["Poisoning in children: Prevention", section on 'Ingested substances'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/poisoning-in-children-prevention?sectionName=Ingested+substances&topicRef=8365&anchor=H108484245&source=see_link#H108484245).)

Rome V diagnostic criteria for cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (April 2026)

Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) is a clinical diagnosis. The Rome V criteria, which update the commonly used Rome IV criteria, were recently published [[28](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/28)]. A patient meets the Rome V criteria for CHS if all of the following are present:

●Stereotypical episodic vomiting resembling cyclic vomiting syndrome in terms of onset, duration, and frequency

●Presentation after prolonged (one year) and excessive cannabis use (≥4 days per week or ≥15 doses per week, or both)

●Relief of vomiting episodes by sustained cessation of cannabis use (at least six months or three typical emetic cycles)

Association with pathologic bathing behavior (prolonged hot baths or showers) is supportive but not necessary. We agree that these criteria can assist in diagnosing CHS. (See ["Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome", section on 'Diagnostic criteria'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/cannabinoid-hyperemesis-syndrome?sectionName=Diagnostic+criteria&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3072534301&source=see_link#H3072534301).)

New recommendations on use of activated charcoal for overdoses (April 2026)

[Activated charcoal](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/activated-charcoal-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) (AC) adsorbs chemicals within minutes of contact, preventing gastrointestinal (GI) absorption and subsequent toxicity. Indications and timing are debatable, and "routine" use for GI decontamination has not demonstrated reduced morbidity and mortality in poisoned patients. Newly released recommendations from the Clinical Toxicology Recommendations Collaborative (which included representatives from three toxicology societies) suggest a potential benefit for a slightly prolonged window for AC administration for ingestion of certain agents (eg, [acetaminophen](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acetaminophen-paracetamol-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), salicylates, and [verapamil](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/verapamil-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link)) and an additional dose of AC for agents with potential for prolonged GI tract persistence (aforementioned agents as well as [carbamazepine](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/carbamazepine-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), [valproic acid](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/valproate-valproic-acid-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), paraquat, [phenobarbital](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/phenobarbital-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), and [theophylline](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/theophylline-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link)) [[29](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/29)]. We agree with most of the recommendations from the Collaborative. (See ["Gastrointestinal decontamination of the poisoned patient", section on 'Indications'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/gastrointestinal-decontamination-of-the-poisoned-patient?sectionName=Indications&topicRef=8365&anchor=H18993776&source=see_link#H18993776).)

Trends in kratom exposures reported to United States poison centers (March 2026)

Kratom (_Mitragyna speciosa_) is a natural product derived from a tree native to Southeast Asia used for its stimulant, analgesic, and antidepressant properties. Commercially sold kratom products can have alkaloidal concentrations that are different compared with natural leaf products, which can cause toxicity and dependence. There were over 14,000 kratom exposures reported to United States poison centers between 2015 and 2025 [[30](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/30)]. Reports steadily increased through 2019, plateaued through 2024, and surged in 2025 (over 3400 reported exposures). Reports involving multiple substances (eg, opioids) were more likely to cause serious outcomes and hospitalization. These findings suggest that kratom-related adverse effects are increasing in the United States. (See ["Kratom health effects from acute and chronic use", section on 'Epidemiology'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/kratom-health-effects-from-acute-and-chronic-use?sectionName=EPIDEMIOLOGY&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2211216297&source=see_link#H2211216297).)

Chronic lead exposure and increased cardiovascular mortality (March 2026)

Cumulative lead exposure has been linked to an increased risk of atherosclerosis, cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality, and all-cause mortality. A study of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey from 1999 to 2014, including over 42,000 individuals, reported that higher estimated bone lead levels were associated with increased CVD mortality; the group with the greatest lead burden had an 88 percent increase in adjusted mortality risk compared with estimated preindustrial levels [[31](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/31)]. This corresponds to an estimated 3.5 million deaths globally in 2023 attributable to elevated bone lead levels, which would account for almost 6 percent of deaths and would make lead exposure the eighth leading risk for global mortality. These findings highlight the need to screen for and mitigate occupational and environmental lead exposure. (See ["Lead exposure, toxicity, and poisoning in adults: Clinical manifestations and diagnosis", section on 'Chronic and long-term exposure effects'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/lead-exposure-toxicity-and-poisoning-in-adults-clinical-manifestations-and-diagnosis?sectionName=Chronic+and+long-term+exposure+effects&topicRef=8365&anchor=H7&source=see_link#H7).)

Causes and prognosis of acquired methemoglobinemia (March 2026)

Acquired methemoglobinemia is a potentially life-threatening condition in which the iron in heme becomes oxidized and cannot deliver oxygen. In a new study from Thailand that evaluated 169 individuals with acquired methemoglobinemia over a 10-year period, the most common causes were [dapsone](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/dapsone-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) (in 30 percent) and the contact herbicide propanil (in 27 percent, mostly for self-harm) [[32](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/32)]. Approximately 10 percent had glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. The fatality rate was 11 percent, 40 percent were admitted to the intensive care unit, 34 percent required intubation, and 89 percent were hospitalized. These data reinforce the importance of rapid recognition and treatment of this condition. (See ["Methemoglobinemia", section on 'Most common acquired causes'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/methemoglobinemia?sectionName=Most+common+acquired+causes&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3113698015&source=see_link#H3113698015).)

Cardiotoxicity of supratherapeutic loperamide exposures (March 2026)

The antidiarrheal agent [loperamide](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/loperamide-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) has been reported to cause ventricular conduction disturbances, including QRS and QT interval prolongation, idioventricular rhythm, and ventricular tachycardia, following overdose. Loperamide is a synthetic opioid but does not typically cause classic signs of opioid toxicity. A systematic review of almost 130 cases of supratherapeutic loperamide exposure found that severe toxicity has been reported at daily doses as low as 20 to 40 mg [[33](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/33)]. Syncope was reported in almost half of cases, while severe cases mainly had polymorphic or sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. These findings suggest that patients with supratherapeutic loperamide exposure may benefit from cardiac monitoring. (See ["Acute opioid intoxication in adults", section on 'Loperamide'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-opioid-intoxication-in-adults?sectionName=Loperamide&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2282453505&source=see_link#H2282453505).)

Psilocybin use in Oregon and Colorado following decriminalization (March 2026)

Psilocybin is a hallucinogen found in many species of mushrooms and has been studied for the treatment of various mental health disorders. Psilocybin was decriminalized for use in licensed clinics in Oregon in 2020 and Colorado in 2022. A study of data from a national survey of drug use from 2018 to 2025 found that self-reported use increased in both states following decriminalization (mean prevalence increased from 2 to 4.5 percent and 2.7 to 4.3 percent in Oregon and Colorado, respectively) [[34](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/34)]. This increase was greater than a weighted composite control of the other states. These findings may impact policy decisions regarding psilocybin decriminalization for therapeutic use. (See ["Intoxication from LSD and other common hallucinogens", section on 'Epidemiology'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/intoxication-from-lsd-and-other-common-hallucinogens?sectionName=EPIDEMIOLOGY&topicRef=8365&anchor=H57999532&source=see_link#H57999532).)

Test characteristics of an enzymatic ethylene glycol assay (March 2026)

Ethylene glycol poisoning is potentially fatal if not treated promptly. Diagnosis can be challenging since ethylene glycol concentrations are usually performed by gas chromatography, which is not widely available and typically has long turn-around times. A modification to a glycerol dehydrogenase-based assay approved for veterinary use has been externally validated and is used by some hospitals; it can be performed 24/7 and has a typical turn-around time of several hours. A study of over 400 samples analyzed by both an enzymatic assay and chromatography found a sensitivity and specificity of 89 and 83 percent, respectively [[35](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/35)]. All four false-negative enzymatic results were below the 20 mg/dL treatment threshold. These results suggest that an enzymatic ethylene glycol assay may be a valuable screening tool. (See ["Methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning: Pharmacology, clinical manifestations, and diagnosis", section on 'Testing for methanol and ethylene glycol'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/methanol-and-ethylene-glycol-poisoning-pharmacology-clinical-manifestations-and-diagnosis?sectionName=Testing+for+methanol+and+ethylene+glycol&topicRef=8365&anchor=H12&source=see_link#H12).)

ED-initiated injectable extended-release buprenorphine (February 2026)

Previous studies have found that emergency department (ED) initiation of sublingual [buprenorphine](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/buprenorphine-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) is associated with decreased all-cause and opioid-related mortality and is feasible and cost-effective. A new trial with almost 2000 ED patients who had untreated opioid use disorder and signs of withdrawal found that ED patients started on extended-release injectable buprenorphine, compared with sublingual buprenorphine, had similar engagement in opioid use disorder treatment at 7 (41 versus 39 percent) and 30 days (44 versus 45 percent) [[36](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/36)]. The rate of precipitated withdrawal was similar and rare (<1 percent) in both groups despite a high prevalence of [fentanyl](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/fentanyl-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) dependence (76 percent). These results suggest that initiation of extended-release injectable buprenorphine may be a safe and feasible option in ED patients for treatment of an opioid use disorder. (See ["Acute opioid intoxication in adults", section on 'Prevention of recurrent opioid overdose'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-opioid-intoxication-in-adults?sectionName=PREVENTION+OF+RECURRENT+OPIOID+OVERDOSE&topicRef=8365&anchor=H10057659&source=see_link#H10057659).)

TRAUMA

Craniotomy for evacuation of intracranial epidural hematoma (July 2026)

Surgical evacuation is often performed in patients with large or symptomatic acute epidural hematomas (EDH) but the optimal surgical approach is uncertain. In an open-label, randomized clinical trial comparing craniotomy and craniectomy in 120 patients with acute traumatic EDH who had transtentorial herniation and a median injury-to-surgery time of 4 hours, favorable functional outcomes at six months were similar between groups (79 and 84 percent, respectively) [[37](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/37)]. Postoperative cerebral infarction and 30-day mortality rates were also similar between groups, but postoperative intracranial hemorrhage was more common in those assigned to craniectomy (36 versus 13 percent). The applicability of these data to patients with more delayed presentations and to those with EDH plus significant cerebral edema or other intracranial pathology is uncertain. These results support the use of craniotomy for surgical evacuation of EDH, even in the setting of transtentorial herniation. (See ["Intracranial epidural hematoma in adults", section on 'Surgical techniques'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/intracranial-epidural-hematoma-in-adults?sectionName=Surgical+techniques&topicRef=8365&anchor=H13&source=see_link#H13).)

Capnography for prognosis in trauma patients (July 2026)

Studies have found that low end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO₂) values in trauma patients on initial medical presentation may indicate a hemorrhagic state and be associated with increased mortality and transfusion requirements. In a meta-analysis with more than 2400 trauma patients, a low EtCO₂ was associated with higher mortality (22 versus 12 percent) and a greater need for transfusion (7 versus 1 percent) [[38](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/38)]. The definition of "low" EtCO₂ ranged from less than 26 to 35 mmHg across the studies, but was less than 30 mmHg in most. These findings suggest that a low EtCO 2 may be a valuable, noninvasive early predictor of severity in trauma patients, but should be used in conjunction with other prognosticators (eg, vital signs, shock index, lactate). (See ["Carbon dioxide monitoring (capnography)", section on 'Increased ICP and trauma prognosis'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/carbon-dioxide-monitoring-capnography?sectionName=Increased+ICP+and+trauma+prognosis&topicRef=8365&anchor=H11&source=see_link#H11).)

PECARN cervical spine injury prediction rule performance by patient age (May 2026)

In a planned subanalysis of the cohort of 22,430 children used to develop the Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) Cervical Spine Injury (CSI) prediction rule ([algorithm 2](https://www.uptodate.com/content-not-available)), age-specific rules were derived based on developmental transition (0 to <2 years, 2 to <8 years, 8 to <16 years, and 16 to <18 years) [[39](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/39)]. When compared with the PECARN CSI rule, testing characteristics were similar for the age-specific rules; the negative predictive value for the PECARN CSI rule (99.9 percent, prevalence of CSI 1.9 percent) equaled or exceeded all age-specific rules. These findings support the use of the PECARN CSI rule to determine the risk of CSI and the need for C-spine imaging in infants and children of all ages. (See ["Evaluation and acute management of cervical spine injuries in children and adolescents", section on 'Indications and choice of imaging'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-acute-management-of-cervical-spine-injuries-in-children-and-adolescents?sectionName=Indications+and+choice+of+imaging&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2844494741&source=see_link#H2844494741).)

Prehospital whole blood transfusion for traumatic hemorrhage (March 2026)

Two recent trials have examined the efficacy and safety of prehospital transfusion of low-titer, group O whole blood (LTOWB) versus blood components by Emergency Medical Services (EMS):

●In a pragmatic trial of over 600 patients with life-threatening bleeding transported by air ambulances in England, patients were transfused up to 2 units of LTOWB versus red cells plus plasma [[40](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/40)]. The composite of mortality plus massive transfusion within 24 hours and 90-day call-cause mortality was similar between the groups; the LTOWB group had slightly fewer serious adverse events.

●In another pragmatic trial of over 1000 patients with trauma and hypotension transported by air bases in the United States, either from the scene or from a referring emergency department, patients were transfused up to 2 units of LTOWB versus red cells, plasma, or both. Mortality at 30 days was similar (26 versus 21 percent) between LTOWB and components, as was in-hospital mortality, blood product requirements, and adverse events [[41](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/41)].

These findings suggest that use of LTOWB, which is logistically simpler than components, is a reasonable option for EMS with prehospital transfusion programs. (See ["Initial management of moderate to severe hemorrhage in the adult trauma patient", section on 'Transfusion'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/initial-management-of-moderate-to-severe-hemorrhage-in-the-adult-trauma-patient?sectionName=Transfusion&topicRef=8365&anchor=H749310297&source=see_link#H749310297).)

## Abstract

In recent years, the incidence of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) has been gradually increasing. Despite advances in supportive care, ARDS remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in critically ill patients. ARDS is characterized by acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure with diffuse pulmonary inflammation and bilateral edema due to excessive alveolocapillary permeability in patients with non-cardiogenic pulmonary diseases. Over the past seven decades, our understanding of the pathology and clinical characteristics of ARDS has evolved significantly, yet it remains an area of active research and discovery. ARDS is highly heterogeneous, including diverse pathological causes, clinical presentations, and treatment responses, presenting a significant challenge for clinicians and researchers. In this review, we comprehensively discuss the latest advancements in ARDS research, focusing on its heterogeneity, pathophysiological mechanisms, and emerging therapeutic approaches, such as cellular therapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy. Moreover, we also examine the pathological characteristics of COVID-19-related ARDS and discuss the corresponding therapeutic approaches. In the face of challenges posed by ARDS heterogeneity, recent advancements offer hope for improved patient outcomes. Further research is essential to translate these findings into effective clinical interventions and personalized treatment approaches for ARDS, ultimately leading to better outcomes for patients suffering from ARDS.
